messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Luis Alvarez, a 70‑year‑old Latino former welder, came to the clinic with a history that began in a small factory in the late 1950s. After a violent union dispute, the plant’s owner had ordered workers to remain in a cramped metal workshop while the building was being burned. Luis was locked inside, surrounded by strangers who shouted, threatened, and, when the fire trucks appeared, fired a single gunshot that echoed through the steel. The sound of that gunshot, the feeling of being trapped and helpless, and the violence he witnessed became the anchors of his lifelong distress. For weeks after the incident, Luis would wake in the dark, the memory of the factory’s walls closing in on him, the taste of metal in his mouth, and the echo of the gunshot in his ears. Those intrusive images were so vivid that, in the days that followed, he could no longer separate them from the present: “It feels like it’s happening right now,” he told me, describing the impossible blend of past and present. He also reported that when he tried to explain what happened, his thoughts would drift: “I start to tell it, but then I lose the thread and can’t finish.” When the memory resurfaced, a fierce rage would surge through him, forcing him to clamp down on his emotions. Luis’s own explanations of the event—“I was there because I had no other option” and “I should have done more”—were the bedrock of his negative appraisals. He believed that anyone could become the next victim, that he would forever live in fear of harm, and that he could never forgive himself for “not doing more.” These beliefs became a vicious loop. Whenever the memory flooded in, he would feel trapped, and the trapped feeling would feed his sense that violence could strike again. The gunshot’s echo would bring the memory back, re‑engaging the same chain. He was certain that the way he had behaved was the reason the torture happened, and this self‑blame reinforced his belief that he had doomed himself and those around him. These negative appraisals in turn drove Luis’s maladaptive coping. When the memory surfaced, he would detach himself from the scene, mentally stepping away from the walls and the sound, as if by doing so he could survive the event again. In social settings, he would become overly compliant—always saying yes to his coworkers, always nodding to authority—because that was the only way he felt safe. When he sensed a threat, he’d suppress thoughts about the past, forcing himself to focus on the task at hand, as if the memory were a poisonous substance he had to keep out of his mind. The gunshot noise, the feeling of entrapment, and the violence of the event were all triggers that sent these coping patterns into motion. Luis’s work as a welder in the 1970s was interrupted by a slow, insidious decline. He avoided standing in the same cramped spots that had once contained him; he would leave the shop before his shifts ended, and when his supervisor asked him to remain after hours, he would leave instead of risking a flashback. These avoidance behaviors had consequences that rippled through his life: his boss reassigned him to lighter duties, and Luis felt increasingly isolated, as if his life was a series of safety zones that could not accommodate him. He also reported that the memory of the factory still made him feel like he could be caught in a second entrapment, and the gunshot’s echo in the night would trigger a new wave of fear and rage, making him doubt whether he would ever feel safe again. When Luis finally sought help, he was exhausted by the endless cycle of fear, rage, and self‑blame. He could no longer stand in the presence of the factory’s metal walls or the memory that lived inside him. He was terrified of hearing a gunshot again, even in a quiet room, and feared that one moment could pull him back into the terror of that day. He hoped that, with treatment, he could break the loop that kept pulling him into the past and relieve the constant threat he felt in the present.
